set.grade.domains.risk_of_bias.note: Blinding is unverifiable or broken in every study read in full (cards sc_krystal_1994, sc_malhotra_1996, sc_newcomer_1999, sc_vollenweider_1997a and sc_vollenweider_1997b, all rated high overall); the review selected each study's peak value by design, and 9 of its 36 studies were not double-blind, 3 of them unblinded. Against the downgrade: blinding status did not change the review's pooled effect significantly in any of the three outcomes, and the review's own across-study summary rates performance and detection bias low. The downgrade is kept, because that is a contrast between studies, no primary study checked whether blinding held, and the peak-value selection is untouched by it.
set.grade.domains.inconsistency.note: I2 75.7%, 74.9% and 64.6% in the review's Results (its abstract prints a range of 77% to 83%, which matches none of them); prediction intervals about 0.28 to 2.72, 0.44 to 2.65 and 0.39 to 1.93 (editors' calculation on the card, reproduced independently by the second reader); the direction is consistent.
set.grade.reasoning: Within-person, placebo-controlled laboratory studies with randomized or counterbalanced order start high (METHODS 6.3; round brief). Risk of bias -1: no study read in full reports a blinding check, the condition produced visible signs in nearly half the people at the larger amount in one study, the main outcomes are clinician ratings and self-ratings, one of the two imaging studies had no dummy condition at all, and the pooled estimates are peak values chosen at each study's largest amount and highest-scoring rating time (the review's confidence is rated low with AMSTAR 2, provisionally, because one item can be judged only from a supplement neither reader opened). The review's own finding that blinding status did not change the pooled effect in any outcome counts against that downgrade; it is kept because the comparison is between studies rather than within them, because no primary study checked whether blinding held, and because the peak-value selection is unaffected by it. Inconsistency -1: heterogeneity across the pooled studies is high (I2 65% to 76% in the Results), subgroup analyses did not explain most of it, and the editors' prediction intervals run from about 0.3 to 2.7, so the size of the effect is uncertain even though its direction is not. Not downgraded for indirectness, because the claim is restricted to healthy volunteers given ketamine into a vein in a laboratory. Not downgraded for imprecision: 725 people and narrow intervals around each pooled estimate. Not downgraded for publication bias, although the Egger tests were significant for all three outcomes, because the trim-and-fill estimates stay large and the claim carries both; a reading that counted that asymmetry as a further downgrade would give very low. Rated as worded, including the size. A claim worded only to the direction and the short duration would sit a level higher, because every one of the 36 pooled studies found an increase and the laboratories read in full agree. Overlapping evidence (METHODS 6.3): Newcomer et al. (1999) is one of the 36 pooled studies, in the total and the positive analyses, so it is not independent of the pooled estimates; Malhotra et al. (1997), a companion report from the laboratory of Malhotra et al. (1996), is pooled as well, while Krystal et al. (1994) is not among the 36; at least 8 of the 36 list a review author among their authors; and the two 1997 studies come from the same Zurich laboratory. How long the effects last is carried by the two studies that rated people again after the infusion stopped, and by nothing else: the review gives no recovery time, states that the time course has still to be characterised, and took its ratings during the session.

evidence_add.extracted: The dummy condition was saline in 35 of the 36 healthy-volunteer studies and not reported in one.
